Comment: SurgiSync web staging - SPA from S3 + /api and /health proxied to the staging ALB

Items._comment: MUST be staging.surgisoftsolutions.com, never the raw ALB hostname. It is the only value that both passes origin TLS validation (the ALB's default listener cert is www-only, so the wildcard is reachable by SNI on this name alone) and produces a Host matching the ALB's priority-10 host-header rule. Any other Host falls to the ALB default rule, which forwards to the PRODUCTION target group - silently, and it looks like it worked.

DefaultCacheBehavior._comment: AWS managed SecurityHeadersPolicy. Verified against the live alias on 2026-08-11, it sends exactly five headers - X-XSS-Protection, X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Strict-Transport-Security - and NO Content-Security-Policy. That absence is load-bearing for Kit Detail's Live Location map, which fetches basemap tiles cross-origin (VITE_MAP_TILE_URL, default tile.openstreetmap.org). Introducing a CSP here without that host in img-src leaves the map an empty grey box on staging while it renders perfectly in dev, because nothing else in the app loads a third-party asset. Leaflet also sets inline style attributes on its tiles and panes, so a CSP would need style-src-attr too. The Referrer-Policy above is separately why OSM sees an identifying origin on tile requests, which their usage policy asks for.

Items._comment: Not optional. /health/data/ is routed at hoosier/urls.py outside /api/, so without this it falls to the S3 behaviour and returns index.html with a 200 - and its "env" field is the cheapest detector for the ALB default-rule trap above. It exposes nothing new; the endpoint is already public on staging.surgisoftsolutions.com.

CustomErrorResponses._comment: TTL-0 only, and deliberately no custom error PAGE - ResponsePagePath is the empty string on every entry, which is CloudFront's way of saying there is none. CloudFront caches 4xx/5xx for 10s even under Managed-CachingDisabled, and that policy excludes the query string from the cache key, so a 503 on ?page=1 could be replayed for ?page=2. An actual response page would be worse than the caching: CustomErrorResponses is distribution-wide, so it would also turn the API's genuine 403s and 404s into a 200 serving index.html. The SPA fallback lives in the viewer-request function instead (infra/spa-router.js). 504 is included because OriginReadTimeout is 60s and gateway timeouts are reachable. Quantity must match the array length. ResponsePagePath and ResponseCode are spelled out rather than omitted: create-distribution defaults them, but update-distribution rejects a partially-specified member of this list with 'The specified list of custom error responses does not exist or is not valid' - so omitting them makes a newly added error code impossible to apply to an existing distribution.
